107	In Victorian England, Lady Ada Lovelace was a friend and collaborator of Charles Babbage, the inventor of the Analytical Engine: the first-known general-purpose mechanical computer. Although visionary and far ahead of its time, the Analytical Engine
108	wasn’t meant as a general-purpose computer when it was designed in the 1830s and
109	1840s, because the concept of general-purpose computation was yet to be invented. It
110	was merely meant as a way to use mechanical operations to automate certain computations from the field of mathematical analysis—hence the name Analytical Engine. As
111	such, it was the intellectual descendant of earlier attempts at encoding mathematical
112	operations in gear form, such as the Pascaline, or Leibniz’s step reckoner, a refined
113	version of the Pascaline. Designed by Blaise Pascal in 1642 (at age 19!), the Pascaline
114	was the world’s first mechanical calculator—it could add, subtract, multiply, or even
115	divide digits.

117	The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do
118	whatever we know how to order it to perform… Its province is to assist us in making
119	available what we’re already acquainted with.

121	arresting. Could a general-purpose computer “originate” anything, or would it always be
122	bound to dully execute processes we humans fully understand? Could it ever be capable

206	A machine learning model transforms its input data into meaningful outputs, a process
207	that is “learned” from exposure to known examples of inputs and outputs. Therefore,
208	the central problem in machine learning and deep learning is to meaningfully transform
209	data: in other words, to learn useful representations of the input data at hand—representations that get us closer to the expected output.
210	Before we go any further, what’s a representation? At its core, it’s a different way to
211	look at data to represent or encode data. For instance, a color image can be encoded in
212	the RGB format (red-green-blue) or in the HSV format (hue-saturation-value): these
213	are two different representations of the same data. Some tasks that may be difficult with
214	one representation can become easy with another. For example, the task “Select all red
215	pixels in the image” is simpler in the RGB format, whereas “Make the image less saturated” is simpler in the HSV format. Machine learning models are all about finding
216	appropriate representations for their input data—transformations of the data that
217	make it more amenable to the task at hand.

267	In this new coordinate system, the coordinates of our points can be said to be a new
268	representation of our data. And it’s a good one! With this representation, the black/

272	In this case, we defined the coordinate change by hand: we used our human intelligence to come up with our own appropriate representation of the data. This is fine for
273	such an extremely simple problem, but could you do the same if the task were to classify images of handwritten digits? Could you write explicit, computer-executable image
274	transformations that would illuminate the difference between a 6 and an 8, between a 1
275	and a 7, across all kinds of different handwritings?
276	This is possible to an extent. Rules based on representations of digits such as “counting the number of closed loops” or vertical and horizontal pixel histograms can do a
277	decent job at telling apart handwritten digits. But finding such useful representations
278	by hand is hard work, and as you can imagine the resulting rule-based system would be
279	brittle and a nightmare to maintain. Every time you would come across a new example
280	of handwriting that would break your carefully thought-out rules, you would have to
281	add new data transformations and new rules, while taking into account their interaction with every previous rule.
282	You’re probably thinking, if this process is so painful, could we automate it? What if
283	we tried systematically searching for different sets of automatically generated representations of the data and rules based on them, identifying good ones using the percentage of digits being correctly classified in some development dataset as feedback? We
284	would then be doing machine learning. Learning, in the context of machine learning,
285	describes an automatic search process for data transformations that produce useful
286	representations of some data, guided by some feedback signal—representations that
287	are amenable to simpler rules solving the task at hand.
288	These transformations can be coordinate changes (like in our 2D coordinates classification example) or a histogram of pixels and counting loops (like in our digits classification example), but they could also be linear projections, translations, and nonlinear
289	operations (such as “Select all points such that x > 0”), and so on. Machine learning
290	algorithms aren’t usually creative in finding these transformations; they’re merely
291	searching through a predefined set of operations, called a hypothesis space. For instance,
292	the space of all possible coordinate changes would be our hypothesis space in the 2D
293	coordinates classification example.
294	So that’s what machine learning is, concisely: searching for useful representations and rules over some input data, within a predefined space of possibilities,
295	using guidance from a feedback signal. This simple idea allows us to solve a remarkably broad range of intellectual tasks, from autonomous driving to natural language
296	question-answering.

307	The “deep” in “deep learning”
308	Deep learning is a specific subfield of machine learning; it’s a new take on learning
309	representations from data, which emphasizes learning successive layers of increasingly
310	meaningful representations. The “deep” in “deep learning” isn’t a reference to any
311	kind of deeper understanding achieved by the approach; rather, it stands for this idea
312	of successive layers of representations. How many layers contribute to a model of the
313	data is called the depth of the model. Other appropriate names for the field could have
314	been layered representations learning or hierarchical representations learning. Modern deep
315	learning often involves tens or even hundreds of successive layers of representations,
316	and they’re all learned automatically from exposure to training data. Meanwhile, other
317	approaches to machine learning tend to focus on learning only one or two layers of
318	representations of the data (say, taking a pixel histogram and then applying a classification rule); hence they’re sometimes called shallow learning.
319	In deep learning, these layered representations are learned via models called neural
320	networks, structured in literal layers stacked on top of each other. The term neural network is a reference to neurobiology, but although some of the central concepts in deep
321	learning were developed in part by drawing inspiration from our understanding of the
322	brain (in particular, the visual cortex), deep learning models are not models of the
323	brain. There’s no evidence that the brain implements anything like the learning mechanisms used in modern deep learning models. You may come across pop science articles proclaiming that deep learning works like the brain or is modeled after the brain,
324	but that isn’t the case. It would be confusing and counterproductive for newcomers
325	to the field to think of deep learning as being in any way related to neurobiology; you
326	don’t need that shroud of “just like our minds” mystique and mystery, and you may as
327	well forget anything you may have read about hypothetical links between deep learning
328	and biology. For our purposes, deep learning is a mathematical framework for learning
329	representations from data.
330	What do the representations learned by a deep learning algorithm look like? Let’s
331	examine how a network several layers deep (see figure 1.5) transforms an image of a
332	digit to recognize what digit it is.

537	What makes deep learning different
538	Is there anything special about deep neural networks that makes them the “right”
539	approach for companies to invest in and for researchers to flock to? Will we still be
540	using deep neural networks in 20 years?
541	Deep learning has several properties that justify its status as an AI revolution, and
542	it’s here to stay. We may not be using neural networks many decades from now, but
543	whatever we use will directly inherit from modern deep learning and its core concepts.
544	These important properties can be broadly sorted into three categories:
545	¡ Simplicity—Deep learning makes problem solving much easier, because it auto-
546	
547	mates what used to be the most crucial step in a machine learning workflow:
548	feature engineering. Previous machine learning techniques—shallow learning—only involved transforming the input data into one or two successive representation spaces, which wasn’t expressive enough for most problems. As such,
549	humans had to go to great lengths to make the initial input data more amenable
550	to processing by these methods: they had to manually engineer good representations for their data. This is called feature engineering. Deep learning, on the other
551	hand, completely automates this step: with deep learning, you learn all features
552	in one pass rather than having to engineer them yourself. This has greatly simplified machine learning workflows, often replacing sophisticated multistage pipelines with a single, simple, end-to-end deep learning model.
553	¡ Scalability—Deep learning is highly amenable to parallelization on GPUs or more
554	specialized machine learning hardware, so it can take full advantage of Moore’s

574	The age of generative AI
575	Perhaps the most well-known example of deep learning today is the recent wave of generative AI applications—chatbot assistants like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, as well
576	as image generation services like Midjourney. These applications have captured the
577	public imagination with their ability to produce informative or even creative content in
578	response to simple prompts, blurring the lines between human and machine creativity.
579	Generative AI is powered by very large “foundation models” that learn to reconstruct
580	the text and image content fed into them—reconstruct a sharp image from a noisy version, predict the next word in a sentence, and so on. This means that the targets from
581	figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself. This is referred to as self-supervised learning,
582	and it enables those models to use vast amounts of unlabeled data. Doing away with the
583	manual data annotations that bottlenecked previous brands of machine learning has
584	unlocked a level of scale never seen before—some of these foundation models have
585	hundreds of billions of parameters and are trained on over 1 petabyte of data, at the
586	cost of tens of millions of dollars.
587	These foundation models operate as a kind of fuzzy database of human knowledge,
588	making them amenable to a very wide range of applications without needing special-­
589	purpose programming or retraining. Because they’ve already memorized so much, they
590	can solve new problems merely via prompting—querying the knowledge representations
591	they’ve learned and returning the output most likely to be associated with your prompt.
592	Generative AI only rose to mainstream awareness in 2022, but it has a long history—
593	the earliest experiments with text generation date back to the 1990s. The first edition
594	of this book, released in 2017, already had a hefty chapter titled “Generative AI” that
595	explored the text generation and image generation techniques of the time, while promising the then-outlandish notion that, “soon,” much of the cultural content we consume
596	would be created with the help of AI.

602	revolution, starting with remarkable results on perceptual tasks from 2013 to 2017,

146	The core building block of neural networks is the layer. You can think of a layer as a
147	filter for data: some data goes in, and it comes out in a more useful form. Specifically,
148	layers extract representations out of the data fed into them—hopefully, representations
149	that are more meaningful for the problem at hand. Most of deep learning consists of
150	chaining together simple layers that will implement a form of progressive data distillation. A deep learning model is like a sieve for data processing, made of a succession of
151	increasingly refined data filters—the layers.

245	Data representations for neural networks
246	In the previous example, we started from data stored in multidimensional NumPy
247	arrays, also called tensors. In general, all current machine learning systems use tensors
248	as their basic data structure. Tensors are fundamental to the field—so fundamental
249	that the TensorFlow framework was named after them. So what’s a tensor?
250	At its core, a tensor is a container for data—usually numerical data. So it’s a container for numbers. You may already be familiar with matrices, which are rank-2 tensors:
251	tensors are a generalization of matrices to an arbitrary number of dimensions (note
252	that in the context of tensors, a dimension is often called an axis).
253	Going over the details of tensors might seem a bit abstract at first. But it’s well worth
254	it—manipulating tensors will be the bread and butter of any machine learning code
255	you ever write.

264	Scalars (rank-0 tensors)
265	A tensor that contains only one number is called a scalar (or scalar tensor, rank-0 tensor, or 0D tensor). In NumPy, a float32 or float64 number is a scalar tensor (or scalar
266	array). You can display the number of axes of a NumPy tensor via the ndim attribute;
267	a scalar tensor has 0 axes (ndim == 0). The number of axes of a tensor is also called its
268	rank. Here’s a NumPy scalar:
269	>>> import numpy as np
270	>>> x = np.array(12)
271	>>> x
272	array(12)
273	>>> x.ndim
274	0
275	
276	2.2.2
277	
278	Vectors (rank-1 tensors)
279	An array of numbers is called a vector (or rank-1 tensor or 1D tensor). A rank-1 tensor
280	has exactly one axis. The following is a NumPy vector:
281	>>> x = np.array([12, 3, 6, 14, 7])
282	>>> x
283	array([12, 3, 6, 14, 7])
284	>>> x.ndim
285	1
286	
287	This vector has five entries and so is called a 5-dimensional vector. Don’t confuse a 5D
288	vector with a 5D tensor! A 5D vector has only one axis and has five dimensions along its
289	axis, whereas a 5D tensor has five axes (and may have any number of dimensions along
290	each axis). Dimensionality can denote either the number of entries along a specific axis
291	(as in the case of our 5D vector) or the number of axes in a tensor (such as a 5D tensor), which can be confusing at times. In the latter case, it’s technically more correct
292	to talk about a tensor of rank 5 (the rank of a tensor being the number of axes), but the
293	ambiguous notation 5D tensor is common regardless.

600	The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
601	Just like any computer program can be ultimately reduced to a small set of binary operations on binary inputs (AND, OR, NOR, and so on), all transformations learned by deep
602	neural networks can be reduced to a handful of tensor operations (or tensor functions)
603	applied to tensors of numeric data. For instance, it’s possible to add tensors, multiply
604	tensors, and so on.
605	In our initial example, we were building our model by stacking Dense layers on top of
606	each other. A Keras layer instance looks like this:
607	keras.layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")
608	
609	This layer can be interpreted as a function, which takes as input a matrix and returns
610	another matrix—a new representation for the input tensor. Specifically, the function is
611	as follows (where W is a matrix and b is a vector, both attributes of the layer):
612	output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)
613	
614	
615	The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations

619	Let’s unpack this. We have three tensor operations here:
620	¡ A tensor product (matmul) between the input tensor and a tensor named W.
621	¡ An addition (+) between the resulting matrix and a vector b.
622	¡ A relu operation: relu(x) is max(x, 0). "relu" stands for “REctified Linear Unit.”
623	
624	Although this section deals entirely with linear algebra expressions, you
625	won’t find any mathematical notation in this book. I’ve found that mathematical concepts can be more readily mastered by programmers with no mathematical background if they’re expressed as short Python snippets instead of

631	Element-wise operations
632	The relu operation and addition are element-wise operations: operations that are
633	applied independently to each entry in the tensors being considered. This means
634	these operations are highly amenable to massively parallel implementations (vectorized
635	implementations, a term that comes from the vector processor supercomputer architecture from the 1970–1990 period). If you want to write a naive Python implementation
636	of an element-wise operation, you use a for loop, as in this naive implementation of an
637	element-wise relu operation:
638	def naive_relu(x):
639	assert len(x.shape) == 2
640	x = x.copy()
641	for i in range(x.shape[0]):
642	for j in range(x.shape[1]):
643	x[i, j] = max(x[i, j], 0)
644	return x
645	
646	x is a rank-2 NumPy tensor.
647	Avoids overwriting
648	the input tensor
649	
650	You could do the same for addition:
651	def naive_add(x, y):
652	assert len(x.shape) == 2
653	assert x.shape == y.shape
654	x = x.copy()
655	for i in range(x.shape[0]):
656	for j in range(x.shape[1]):
657	x[i, j] += y[i, j]
658	return x

660	x and y are rank-2 NumPy tensors.
661	Avoids overwriting the input tensor

665	well-optimized built-in NumPy functions, which themselves delegate the heavy lifting

1220	Step 1 sounds easy enough—it’s just I/O code. Steps 2 and 3 are merely the application of a handful of tensor operations, so you could implement these steps purely from
1221	what you learned in the previous section. The difficult part is step 4: updating the model’s weights. Given an individual weight coefficient in the model, how can you compute
1222	whether the coefficient should be increased or decreased, and by how much?
1223	One naive solution would be to freeze all weights in the model except the one scalar
1224	coefficient being considered and try different values for this coefficient. Let’s say the
1225	initial value of the coefficient is 0.3. After the forward pass on a batch of data, the loss of
1226	the model on the batch is 0.5. If you change the coefficient’s value to 0.35 and rerun the
1227	forward pass, the loss increases to 0.6. But if you lower the coefficient to 0.25, the loss
1228	falls to 0.4. In this case, it seems that updating the coefficient by –0.05 would contribute
1229	to minimizing the loss. This would have to be repeated for all coefficients in the model.
1230	But such an approach would be horribly inefficient because you’d need to compute
1231	two forward passes (which are expensive) for every individual coefficient (of which
1232	there are many, usually at least a few thousands and potentially up to billions). Thankfully, there’s a much better approach: gradient descent.
1233	Gradient descent is the optimization technique that powers modern neural networks. Here’s the gist of it. All of the functions used in our models (such as matmul or
1234	+) transform their input in a smooth and continuous way: if you look at z = x + y, for
1235	instance, a small change in y only results in a small change in z, and if you know the
1236	direction of the change in y, you can infer the direction of the change in z. Mathematically, you’d say these functions are differentiable. If you chain together such functions, the bigger function you obtain is still differentiable. In particular, this applies to
1237	the function that maps the model’s coefficients to the loss of the model on a batch of
1238	data: a small change of the model’s coefficients results in a small, predictable change
1239	of the loss value. This enables you to use a mathematical operator called the gradient to
1240	describe how the loss varies as you move the model’s coefficients in different directions.
1241	If you compute this gradient, you can use it to move the coefficients (all at once in a single update, rather than one at a time) in a direction that decreases the loss.

1543	Chaining derivatives: The Backpropagation algorithm
1544	In the previously discussed algorithm, we casually assumed that because a function is
1545	differentiable, we can easily compute its gradient. But is that true? How can we compute the gradient of complex expressions in practice? In our two-layer network example, how can we get the gradient of the loss with regard to the weights? That’s where
1546	the Backpropagation algorithm comes in.
1547	The chain rule
1548	
1549	Backpropagation is a way to use the derivative of simple operations (such as addition,
1550	relu, or tensor product) to easily compute the gradient of arbitrarily complex combinations of these atomic operations. Crucially, a neural network consists of many tensor operations chained together, each of which has a simple, known derivative. For
1551	instance, the model from our first example can be expressed as a function parameterized by the variables W1, b1, W2, and b2 (belonging to the first and second Dense layers,
1552	respectively), involving the atomic operations matmul, relu, softmax, and +, as well as
1553	our loss function, loss, which are all easily differentiable:
1554	loss_value = loss(
1555	y_true,
1556	softmax(matmul(relu(matmul(inputs, W1) + b1), W2) + b2),
1557	)
1558	
1559	Calculus tells us that such a chain of functions can be derived using the following identity, called the chain rule. Consider two functions f and g, as well as the composed function fg such that y = fg(x) == f(g(x)):

1571	Then the chain rule states that grad(y, x) == grad(y, x1) * grad(x1, x). This enables
1572	you to compute the derivative of fg as long as you know the derivatives of f and g. The
1573	chain rule is named like this because when you add more intermediate functions, it
1574	starts looking like a chain:
1575	def fghj(x):

1583	Applying the chain rule to the computation of the gradient values of a neural network
1584	gives rise to an algorithm called backpropagation. Let’s see how that works, concretely.
1585	Automatic differentiation with computation graphs
1586	
1587	A useful way to think about backpropagation is in terms of computation graphs. A computation graph is the data structure at the heart of the deep learning revolution. It’s
1588	a directed acyclic graph of operations—in our case, tensor operations. For instance,
1589	figure 2.21 is the graph representation of our first model.
1590	Computation graphs have been an extremely successful abstraction in computer
1591	science because they enable us to treat computation as data: a computable expression is
1592	encoded as a machine-readable data structure that can be used as the input or output of
1593	another program. For instance, you could imagine a program that receives a computation
1594	graph and returns a new computation graph that implements a large-scale distributed version of the same computation—this would mean that you could distribute any computation without having to write the distribution logic yourself. Or imagine … a program that
1595	receives a computation graph and can automatically generate the derivative of the expression it represents. It’s much easier to do these things if your computation is expressed as an
1596	explicit graph data structure rather than, say, lines of ASCII characters in a .py file.

43	In the real world, you’re not going to be writing low-level code from scratch like we did

47	If you’re just getting started with deep learning, it may seem like all these frameworks
48	have been here forever. In reality, they’re all quite recent, with Keras being the oldest
49	among the four (launched in March 2015). The ideas behind these frameworks, however, have a long history—the first paper about automatic differentiation was published

69	neural networks that could run on consumer GPUs. The initial focus on CUDA was on

345	
346	So far, TensorFlow seems to look a lot like NumPy. But here’s something NumPy
347	can’t do: retrieve the gradient of any differentiable expression with respect to any of

349	input tensors, and retrieve the gradient of the result with respect to the inputs.
350	Listing 3.10 Using the GradientTape

357	to its weights: gradients = tape.gradient(loss, weights).

359	inputs and how inputs could be either scalars or high-dimensional tensors.

363	you’d have to manually mark it as being tracked, by calling tape.watch() on it.

402	Making TensorFlow functions fast using compilation
403	
404	All the TensorFlow code you’ve written so far has been executing “eagerly.” This means
405	operations are executed one after the other in the Python runtime, much like any
406	Python code or NumPy code. Eager execution is great for debugging, but it is typically quite slow. It can often be beneficial to parallelize some computation, or “fuse”
407	operations—replacing two consecutive operations, like matmul followed by relu, with
408	a single, more efficient operation that does the same thing without materializing the
409	intermediate output.
410	This can be achieved via compilation. The general idea of compilation is to take certain functions you’ve written in Python, lift them out of Python, automatically rewrite
411	them into a faster and more efficient “compiled program,” and then call that program
412	from the Python runtime.
413	The main benefit of compilation is improved performance. There’s a drawback too:
414	the code you write is no longer the code that gets executed, which can make the debugging experience painful. Only turn on compilation after you’ve already debugged your
415	code in the Python runtime.
416	You can apply compilation to any TensorFlow function by wrapping it in a tf.function
417	decorator, like this:
418	@tf.function
419	def dense(inputs, W, b):
420	return tf.nn.relu(tf.matmul(inputs, W) + b)
421	
422	When you do this, any call to dense() is replaced with a call to a compiled program that
423	implements a more optimized version of the function. The first call to the function will
424	take a bit longer, because TensorFlow will be compiling your code. This only happens
425	once—all subsequent calls to the same function will be fast.
426	TensorFlow has two compilation modes:
427	
428	
429	Introduction to TensorFlow

431	69
432	
433	¡ First, the default one, which we refer to as “graph mode.” Any function decorated
434	
435	with @tf.function runs in graph mode.
436	¡ Second, compilation with XLA, a high-performance compiler for ML (it’s
437	short for Accelerated Linear Algebra). You can turn it on by specifying jit_
438	compile=True, like this:
439	@tf.function(jit_compile=True)
440	def dense(inputs, W, b):
441	return tf.nn.relu(tf.matmul(inputs, W) + b)
442	
443	It is often the case that compiling a function with XLA will make it run faster than
444	graph mode—though it takes more time to execute the function the first time, since
445	the compiler has more work to do.

1076	Introduction to JAX
1077	JAX is an open source library for differentiable computation, primarily developed by
1078	Google. After its release in 2018, JAX quickly gained traction in the research community, particularly for its ability to use Google’s TPUs at scale. Today, JAX is in use by

1080	Midjourney, Anthropic, Cohere, and so on.

1082	not maintain any persistent state. This contrasts with traditional imperative programming, where variables can hold values between function calls.

1084	effective automatic parallelization and distributed computation, as functions can be
1085	executed independently without the need for synchronization. The extreme scalability
1086	of JAX is essential for handling the very large-scale machine learning problems faced by
1087	companies like Google and DeepMind.

1133	operations. We said earlier that JAX is stateless, which implies that JAX code can’t rely
1134	on any hidden global state. Consider the following NumPy code.

1483	The main thing that makes JAX unique among modern machine learning frameworks
1484	is its functional, stateless philosophy. While it may seem to cause friction at first, it is
1485	what unlocks the power of JAX—its ability to compile to extremely fast code and to
1486	scale to arbitrarily large models and arbitrarily many devices.
1487	There’s a lot to like about JAX:
1488	¡ It’s fast. For most models, it is the fastest of all frameworks you’ve seen so far.
1489	¡ Its numerical API is fully consistent with NumPy, making it pleasant to learn.
1490	¡ It’s the best fit for training models on TPUs, as it was developed from the ground
1491	
1492	up for XLA and TPUs.
1493	Using JAX can also come with some amount of developer friction:
1494	¡ Its use of metaprogramming and compilation can make it significantly harder to
1495	
1496	debug compared to pure eager execution.
1497	¡ Low-level training loops tend to be more verbose and more difficult to write than
1498

1633	Layers: The building blocks of deep learning
1634	The fundamental data structure in neural networks is the layer, to which you were
1635	introduced in chapter 2. A layer is a data processing module that takes as input one or
1636	more tensors and that outputs one or more tensors. Some layers are stateless, but more
1637	frequently layers have a state: the layer’s weights, one or several tensors learned with stochastic gradient descent, which together contain the network’s knowledge.

1644	Different types of layers are appropriate for different tensor formats and different
1645	types of data processing. For instance, simple vector data, stored in 2D tensors of shape
1646	(samples, features), is often processed by densely connected layers, also called fully connected or dense layers (the Dense class in Keras). Sequence data, stored in 3D tensors of
1647	shape (samples, timesteps, features), is typically processed by recurrent layers, such as
1648	an LSTM layer, or 1D convolution layers (Conv1D). Image data, stored in rank-4 tensors,
1649	is usually processed by 2D convolution layers (Conv2D).
1650	You can think of layers as the LEGO bricks of deep learning, a metaphor that is made
1651	explicit by Keras. Building deep learning models in Keras is done by clipping together
1652	compatible layers to form useful data transformation pipelines.

1659	forward pass). The weights are typically defined in a build() (although they could also
1660	be created in the constructor __init__()), and the computation is defined in the call()
1661	method.

1814	From layers to models
1815	A deep learning model is a graph of layers. In Keras, that’s the Model class. For now,
1816	you’ve only seen Sequential models (a subclass of Model), which are simple stacks of
1817	layers, mapping a single input to a single output. But as you move forward, you’ll be
1818	exposed to a much broader variety of network topologies. Some common ones are
1819	¡ Two-branch networks
1820	¡ Multihead networks
1821	¡ Residual connections

1823	Network topology can get quite involved. For instance, figure 3.5 shows topology of the
1824	graph of layers of a Transformer, a common architecture designed to process text data.
1825	There are generally two ways of building such models in Keras: you can directly subclass the Model class, or you can use the Functional API, which lets you do more with less
1826	code. We’ll cover both approaches in chapter 7.
1827	The topology of a model defines a hypothesis space. You may remember that in chapter 1, we described machine learning as “searching for useful representations of some
1828	input data, within a predefined space of possibilities, using guidance from a feedback signal.” By choosing a network topology, you constrain your space of possibilities (hypothesis space) to a specific series of tensor operations, mapping input data to output data.
1829	What you’ll then be searching for is a good set of values for the weight tensors involved
1830	in these tensor operations.
1831	To learn from data, you have to make assumptions about it. These assumptions
1832	define what can be learned. As such, the structure of your hypothesis space—the architecture of your model—is extremely important. It encodes the assumptions you make
1833	about your problem, the prior knowledge that the model starts with. For instance, if
1834	you’re working on a two-class classification problem with a model made of a single Dense
1835	layer with no activation (a pure affine transformation), you are assuming that your two
1836	classes are linearly separable.
1837	Picking the right network architecture is more an art than a science, and although
1838	there are some best practices and principles you can rely on, only practice can help you
1839	become a proper neural network architect. The next few chapters will both teach you
1840	explicit principles for building neural networks and help you develop intuition as to

1980	Picking a loss function
1981	Choosing the right loss function for the right problem is extremely important: your
1982	network will take any shortcut it can to minimize the loss. So if the objective doesn’t
1983	fully correlate with success for the task at hand, your network will end up doing things
1984	you may not have wanted. Imagine a stupid, omnipotent AI trained via SGD, with this
1985	poorly chosen objective function: “Maximize the average well-being of all humans
1986	alive.” To make its job easier, this AI might choose to kill all humans except a few and
1987	focus on the well-being of the remaining ones because average well-being isn’t affected
1988	by how many humans are left. That might not be what you intended! Just remember
1989	that all neural networks you build will be just as ruthless in lowering their loss function,
1990	so choose the objective wisely, or you’ll have to face unintended side effects.
1991	Fortunately, when it comes to common problems such as classification, regression,
1992	and sequence prediction, there are simple guidelines you can follow to choose the

246	The input data is vectors, and the labels are scalars (1s and 0s): this is one of the simplest problem setups you’ll ever encounter. A type of model that performs well on such
247	a problem is a plain stack of densely connected (Dense) layers with relu activations.

249	layers:
250	¡ How many layers to use

255	¡ Two intermediate layers with 16 units each

293	The first argument being passed to each Dense layer is the number of units in the layer:
294	the dimensionality of representation space of the layer. You remember from chapters 2
295	and 3 that each such Dense layer with a relu activation implements the following chain
296	of tensor operations:
297	output = relu(dot(input, W) + b)
298	
299	Having 16 units means the weight matrix W will have shape (input_dimension, 16): the
300	dot product with W will project the input data onto a 16-dimensional representation
301	space (and then you’ll add the bias vector b and apply the relu operation). You can
302	intuitively understand the dimensionality of your representation space as “how much
303	freedom you’re allowing the model to have when learning internal representations.”
304	Having more units (a higher-dimensional representation space) allows your model to
305	learn more complex representations, but it makes the model more computationally
306	expensive and may lead to learning unwanted patterns (patterns that will improve performance on the training data but not on the test data).
307	The intermediate layers use relu as their activation function, and the final layer uses
308	a sigmoid activation to output a probability (a score between 0 and 1, indicating how
309	likely the review is to be positive). A relu (rectified linear unit) is a function meant to
310	zero-out negative values (see figure 4.2), whereas a sigmoid “squashes” arbitrary values
311	into the [0, 1] interval (see figure 4.3), outputting something that can be interpreted
312	as a probability.
313	
314	What are activation functions, and why are they necessary?
315	Without an activation function like relu (also called a non-linearity), the Dense layer
316	would consist of two linear operations—a dot product and an addition:
317

323	(continued)
324	output = dot(input, W) + b
325	
326	So the layer could only learn linear transformations (affine transformations) of the
327	input data: the hypothesis space of the layer would be the set of all possible linear
328	transformations of the input data into a 16-dimensional space. Such a hypothesis
329	space is too restricted and wouldn’t benefit from multiple layers of representations
330	because a deep stack of linear layers would still implement a linear operation: adding
331	more layers wouldn’t extend the hypothesis space (as you saw in chapter 2).
332	To get access to a much richer hypothesis space that would benefit from deep representations, you need a non-linearity or activation function. relu is the most popular
333	activation function in deep learning, but there are many other candidates, which all
334	come with similarly strange names: prelu, elu, and so on.

344	Finally, you need to choose a loss function and an optimizer. Because you’re facing
345	a binary classification problem and the output of your model is a probability (you
346	end your model with a single-unit layer with a sigmoid activation), it’s best to use the
347	binary_crossentropy loss. It isn’t the only viable choice: you could use, for instance,
348	mean_squared_error. But crossentropy is usually the best choice when you’re dealing
349	with models that output probabilities. Crossentropy is a quantity from the field of information theory that measures the distance between probability distributions or, in this
350	case, between the ground-truth distribution and your predictions.
351	As for the choice of the optimizer, we’ll go with adam, which is usually a good default
352	choice for virtually any problem.

370	Validating your approach
371	As you learned in chapter 3, a deep learning model should never be evaluated on its
372	training data—it’s standard practice to use a “validation set” to monitor the accuracy of
373	the model during training. Here, you’ll create a validation set by setting apart 10,000
374	samples from the original training data.
375	You might ask, why not simply use the test data to evaluate the model? That seems like
376	it would be easier. The reason is that you’re going to want to use the results you get on
377	the validation set to inform your next choices to improve training—for instance, your
378	choice of what model size to use or how many epochs to train for. When you start doing
379	this, your validation scores stop being an accurate reflection of the performance of the
380	model on brand-new data, since the model has been deliberately modified to perform
381	better on the validation data. It’s good to keep around a set of never-before-seen samples that you can use to perform the final evaluation round in a completely unbiased
382	way, and that’s exactly what the test set is. We’ll talk more about this in the next chapter.

485	As you can see, the training loss decreases with every epoch, and the training accuracy increases with every epoch. That’s what you would expect when running gradient-­

571	Wrapping up
572	Here’s what you should take away from this example:
573	¡ You usually need to do quite a bit of preprocessing on your raw data to be able to
574	
575	feed it—as tensors—into a neural network. Sequences of words can be encoded
576	as binary vectors, but there are other encoding options, too.
577	¡ Stacks of Dense layers with relu activations can solve a wide range of problems
578	
579	(including sentiment classification), and you’ll use them frequently.
580	¡ In a binary classification problem (two output classes), your model should end
581	
582	with a Dense layer with one unit and a sigmoid activation: the output of your
583	model should be a scalar between 0 and 1, encoding a probability.
584	¡ With such a scalar sigmoid output on a binary classification problem, the loss
585	
586	function you should use is binary_crossentropy.
587	¡ The adam optimizer is generally a good enough choice, whatever your problem.
588	
589	That’s one less thing for you to worry about.
590	¡ As they get better on their training data, neural networks eventually start overfitting
591	
592	and end up obtaining increasingly worse results on data they’ve never seen before.
593	Be sure to always monitor performance on data that is outside of the training set!

597	Classifying newswires: A multiclass classification example
598	In the previous section, you saw how to classify vector inputs into two mutually exclusive classes using a densely connected neural network. But what happens when you
599	have more than two classes?
600	In this section, you’ll build a model to classify Reuters newswires into 46 mutually
601	exclusive topics. Because you have many classes, this problem is an instance of multiclass
602	classification, and because each data point should be classified into only one category,
603	the problem is more specifically an instance of single-label, multiclass classification. If each
604	data point could belong to multiple categories (in this case, topics), you’d be facing a
605	multilabel, multiclass classification problem.
606	
607	4.2.1

698	Building your model
699	This topic classification problem looks similar to the previous movie review classification problem: in both cases, you’re trying to classify short snippets of text. But there is
700	a new constraint here: the number of output classes has gone from 2 to 46. The dimensionality of the output space is much larger.
701	In a stack of Dense layers like those you’ve been using, each layer can only access
702	information present in the output of the previous layer. If one layer drops some
703	information relevant to the classification problem, this information can never be

711	16-dimensional space may be too limited to learn to separate 46 different classes:
712	such small layers may act as information bottlenecks, permanently dropping relevant
713	information.
714	For this reason, you’ll use larger intermediate layers. Let’s go with 64 units.

724	There are two other things you should note about this architecture:
725	¡ You end the model with a Dense layer of size 46. This means for each input sam-
726	
727	ple, the network will output a 46-dimensional vector. Each entry in this vector
728	(each dimension) will encode a different output class.
729	¡ The last layer uses a softmax activation. You saw this pattern in the MNIST exam-
730	
731	ple. It means the model will output a probability distribution over the 46 different
732	output classes—for every input sample, the model will produce a 46-dimensional
733	output vector, where output[i] is the probability that the sample belongs to class
734	i. The 46 scores will sum to 1.
735	The best loss function to use in this case is categorical_crossentropy. It measures the
736	distance between two probability distributions—here, between the probability distribution outputted by the model and the true distribution of the labels. By minimizing
737	the distance between these two distributions, you train the model to output something
738	as close as possible to the true labels.
739	Like last time, we’ll also monitor accuracy. However, accuracy is a bit of a crude
740	metric in this case: if the model has the correct class as its second choice for a given
741	sample, with an incorrect first choice, the model will still have an accuracy of zero on
742	that sample—even though such a model would be much better than a random guess.
743	A more nuanced metric in this case is top-k accuracy, such as top-3 or top-5 accuracy. It
744	measures whether the correct class was among the top-k predictions of the model. Let’s
745	add top-3 accuracy to our model.

1091	Preparing the data
1092	It would be problematic to feed into a neural network values that all take wildly different ranges. The model might be able to automatically adapt to such heterogeneous
1093	data, but it would definitely make learning more difficult. A widespread best practice
1094	to deal with such data is to do feature-wise normalization: for each feature in the input
1095	data (a column in the input data matrix), you subtract the mean of the feature and
1096	divide by the standard deviation, so that the feature is centered around 0 and has a unit
1097	standard deviation. This is easily done in NumPy.
1098	Listing 4.25 Normalizing the data
1099	mean = train_data.mean(axis=0)
1100	std = train_data.std(axis=0)
1101	x_train = (train_data - mean) / std
1102	x_test = (test_data - mean) / std
1103	
1104	Note that the quantities used for normalizing the test data are computed using the
1105	training data. You should never use in your workflow any quantity computed on the
1106	test data, even for something as simple as data normalization.
1107	In addition, we should also scale the targets. Our normalized inputs have their value
1108	in a small range close to 0, and our model’s weights are initialized with small random
1109	values. This means that our model’s prediction will also be small values when we start
1110	training. If the targets are in the range 60,000–500,000, the model is going to need very
1111	large weight values to output those. With a small learning rate, it would take a very long
1112	time to get there. The simplest fix is to divide all target values by 100,000, so that the
1113	smallest target becomes 0.6, and the largest becomes 5. We can then convert the model’s predictions back to dollar values by multiplying them by 100,000 accordingly.

1166	Validating your approach using K-fold validation
1167	To evaluate your model while you keep adjusting its parameters (such as the number
1168	of epochs used for training), you could split the data into a training set and a validation
1169	set, as you did in the previous examples. But because you have so few data points, the
1170	validation set would end up being very small (for instance, about 100 examples). As a
1171	consequence, the validation scores might change a lot depending on which data points
1172	you chose to use for validation and which you chose for training: the validation scores
1173	might have a high variance with regard to the validation split. This would prevent you
1174	from reliably evaluating your model.
1175	The best practice in such situations is to use K-fold cross-validation (see figure 4.9).
1176	It consists of splitting the available data into K partitions (typically K = 4 or 5), instantiating K identical models, and training each one on K – 1 partitions while evaluating on
1177	the remaining partition. The validation score for the model used is then the average of
1178	the K validation scores obtained. In terms of code, this is straightforward.

39	they were trained on quickly became evident: after just a few epochs, performance

43	The fundamental issue in machine learning is the tension between optimization and
44	generalization. Optimization refers to the process of adjusting a model to get the best
45	performance possible on the training data (the learning in machine learning), whereas
46	generalization refers to how well the trained model performs on data it has never seen
47	before. The goal of the game is to get good generalization, of course, but you don’t control generalization; you can only fit the model to its training data. If you do that too well,
48	overfitting kicks in and generalization suffers.

148	Likewise, machine learning models trained on datasets that include rare feature values are highly susceptible to overfitting. In a sentiment classification task, if the word

324	The manifold hypothesis
325	
326	The input to an MNIST classifier (before preprocessing) is a 28 × 28 array of integers
327	between 0 and 255. The total number of possible input values is thus 256 to the power
328	of 784—much greater than the number of atoms in the universe. However, very few
329	of these inputs would look like valid MNIST samples: actual handwritten digits only
330	occupy a tiny subspace of the parent space of all possible 28 × 28 uint8 arrays. What’s
331	more, this subspace isn’t just a set of points sprinkled at random in the parent space: it
332	is highly structured.
333	First, the subspace of valid handwritten digits is continuous: if you take a sample and
334	modify it a little, it will still be recognizable as the same handwritten digit. Further, all
335	samples in the valid subspace are connected by smooth paths that run through the subspace. This means that if you take two random MNIST digits A and B, there exists a
336	sequence of “intermediate” images that morph A into B, such that two consecutive digits are very close to each other (see figure 5.7). Perhaps there will be a few ambiguous
337	shapes close to the boundary between two classes, but even these shapes would still look
338	very digit-like.
339	
340	Figure 5.7 Different MNIST digits gradually morphing into one another, showing that the space of
341	handwritten digits forms a “manifold.” This image was generated using code from chapter 17.
342	
343	In technical terms, you would say that handwritten digits form a manifold within the
344	space of possible 28 × 28 uint8 arrays. That’s a big word, but the concept is pretty intuitive. A manifold is a lower-dimensional subspace of some parent space that is locally
345	similar to a linear (Euclidean) space. For instance, a smooth curve in the plane is a 1D
346	manifold within a 2D space because for every point of the curve, you can draw a tangent (the curve can be approximated by a line in every point). A smooth surface within
347	a 3D space is a 2D manifold. And so on.
348	More generally, the manifold hypothesis posits that all natural data lies on a low-­
349	dimensional manifold within the high-dimensional space where it is encoded. That’s
350	a pretty strong statement about the structure of information in the universe. As far as
351	we know, it’s accurate, and it’s the reason why deep learning works. It’s true for MNIST

400	time, and they do just fine. You don’t need to be trained in advance on countless examples of every situation you’ll ever have to encounter. Every single one of your days is
401	different from any day you’ve experienced before, and different from any day experienced by anyone since the dawn of humanity. You can switch between spending a week
402	in NYC, a week in Shanghai, and a week in Bangalore without requiring thousands of
403	lifetimes of learning and rehearsal for each city.
404	Humans are capable of extreme generalization, which is enabled by cognitive mechanisms other than interpolation—abstraction, symbolic models of the world, reasoning,
405	logic, common sense, innate priors about the world—what we generally call reason, as

415	Why deep learning works
416	
417	Remember the crumpled paper ball metaphor from chapter 2? A sheet of paper represents a 2D manifold within 3D space (figure 5.9). A deep learning model is a tool for
418	uncrumpling paper balls—that is, for disentangling latent manifolds.
419	
420	Figure 5.9 Uncrumpling a
421	complicated manifold of data
422	
423	A deep learning model is basically a very high-dimensional curve. The curve is smooth
424	and continuous (with additional constraints on its structure, originating from model
425	architecture priors) because it needs to be differentiable. And that curve is fitted to
426	data points via gradient descent—smoothly and incrementally. By construction, deep
427	learning is about taking a big, complex curve—a manifold—and incrementally adjusting its parameters until it fits some training data points.
428	The curve involves enough parameters that it could fit anything. Indeed, if you let
429	your model train for long enough, it will effectively end up purely memorizing its training data and won’t generalize at all. However, the data you’re fitting to isn’t made of isolated points sparsely distributed across the underlying space. Your data forms a highly
430	structured, low-dimensional manifold within the input space—that’s the manifold
431	hypothesis. And because fitting your model curve to this data happens gradually and
432	smoothly over time, as gradient descent progresses, there will be an intermediate point
433	during training at which the model roughly approximates the natural manifold of the
434	data, as you can see in figure 5.10.
435	Moving along the curve learned by the model at that point will come close to moving
436	along the actual latent manifold of the data. As such, the model will be capable of making sense of never-before-seen inputs via interpolation between training inputs.
437	Besides the trivial fact that they have sufficient representational power, there are a
438	few properties of deep learning models that make them particularly well suited to learning latent manifolds:
439	¡ Deep learning models implement a smooth, continuous mapping from their
440	
441	inputs to their outputs. It has to be smooth and continuous because it must
442	be differentiable, by necessity (you couldn’t do gradient descent otherwise).
443	This smoothness helps approximate latent manifolds, which follow the same
444	properties.

487	Training data is paramount
488	
489	While deep learning is indeed well suited to manifold learning, the power to generalize is more a consequence of the natural structure of your data than a consequence
490	of any property of your model. You’ll only be able to generalize if your data forms a
491	manifold where points can be interpolated. The more informative and the less noisy
492	your features are, the better you will be able to generalize, since your input space will
493	be simpler and better structured. Data curation and feature engineering are essential
494	to generalization.
495	Further, because deep learning is curve fitting, for a model to perform well, it needs to
496	be trained on a dense sampling of its input space. A “dense sampling” in this context means
497	that the training data should densely cover the entirety of the input data manifold (see
498	figure 5.11). This is especially true near decision boundaries. With a sufficiently dense

525	As such, you should always keep in mind that the best way to improve a deep learning
526	model is to train it on more data or better data (of course, adding overly noisy or inaccurate data will harm generalization). A denser coverage of the input data manifold
527	will yield a model that generalizes better. You should never expect a deep learning

529	priors encoded in its architecture and the data it was trained on.

531	quantity of information that your model is allowed to store, or to add constraints on the
532	smoothness of the model curve. If a network can only afford to memorize a small number of patterns, or very regular patterns, the optimization process will force it to focus
533	on the most prominent patterns, which have a better chance of generalizing well. The
534	process of fighting overfitting this way is called regularization. We’ll review regularization
535	techniques in depth in section 5.4.4.

548	Evaluating machine-learning models
549	You can only control what you can observe. Since your goal is to develop models that
550	can successfully generalize to new data, it’s essential to be able to reliably measure the
551	generalization power of your model. In this section, we’ll formally introduce the different ways you can evaluate machine learning models. You’ve already seen most of them
552	in action in the previous chapter.
553	
554	5.2.1
555	
556	Training, validation, and test sets
557	Evaluating a model always boils down to splitting the available data into three sets:
558	training, validation, and test. You train on the training data and evaluate your model
559	on the validation data. Once your model is ready for prime time, you test it one final
560	time on the test data, which is meant to be as similar as possible to production data.
561	Then you can deploy the model in production.
562	You may ask, why not have two sets: a training set and a test set? You’d train on the
563	training data and evaluate on the test data. Much simpler!
564	The reason is that developing a model always involves tuning its configuration: for
565	example, choosing the number of layers or the size of the layers (called the hyperparameters of the model, to distinguish them from the parameters, which are the network’s
566	weights). You do this tuning by using as a feedback signal the performance of the model
567	on the validation data. In essence, this tuning is a form of learning: a search for a good
568	configuration in some parameter space. As a result, tuning the configuration of the
569	model based on its performance on the validation set can quickly result in overfitting to
570	the validation set, even though your model is never directly trained on it.
571	Central to this phenomenon is the notion of information leaks. Every time you tune
572	a hyperparameter of your model based on the model’s performance on the validation
573	set, some information about the validation data leaks into the model. If you do this only
574	once, for one parameter, then very few bits of information will leak, and your validation
575	set will remain reliable to evaluate the model. But if you repeat this many times—
576	running one experiment, evaluating on the validation set, and modifying your model as
577	a result—then you’ll leak an increasingly significant amount of information about the
578	validation set into the model.
579	At the end of the day, you’ll end up with a model that performs artificially well on the
580	validation data because that’s what you optimized it for. You care about performance on
581	completely new data, not the validation data, so you need to use a completely different,
582	never-before-seen dataset to evaluate the model: the test dataset. Your model shouldn’t
583	have had access to any information about the test set, even indirectly. If anything about
584	the model has been tuned based on test set performance, then your measure of generalization will be flawed.
585	Splitting your data into training, validation, and test sets may seem straightforward, but there are a few advanced ways to do it that can come in handy when little
586	data is available. Let’s review three classic evaluation recipes: simple hold-out validation, K-fold validation, and iterated K-fold validation with shuffling. We’ll also

762	5.2.2
763	
764	Beating a common-sense baseline
765	Besides the different evaluation protocols you have available, one last thing you should
766	know about is the use of common-sense baselines.
767	Training a deep learning model is a bit like pressing a button that launches a rocket
768	in a parallel world. You can’t hear it or see it. You can’t observe the manifold learning
769	process—it’s happening in a space with thousands of dimensions, and even if you projected it to 3D, you couldn’t interpret it. The only feedback you have is your validation
770	metrics—like an altitude meter on your invisible rocket.
771	A particularly important point is to be able to tell whether you’re getting off the
772	ground at all. What was the altitude you started at? Your model seems to have an accuracy of 15%, is that any good? Before you start working with a dataset, you should always
773	pick a trivial baseline that you’ll try to beat. If you cross that threshold, you’ll know
774	you’re doing something right: your model is actually using the information in the input
775	data to make predictions that generalize—you can keep going. This baseline could be
776	performance of a random classifier, or the performance of the simplest non-machine
777	learning technique you can imagine.
778	For instance, in the MNIST digit-classification example, a simple baseline would be a
779	validation accuracy greater than 0.1 (random classifier); in the IMDB example, it would
780	be a validation accuracy greater than 0.5. In the Reuters example, it would be around
781	0.18–0.19, due to class imbalance. If you have a binary classification problem where 90%
782	of samples belong to class A and 10% belong to class B, then a classifier that always predicts A already achieves 0.9 in validation accuracy, and you’ll need to do better than that.
783	Having a common sense baseline you can refer to is essential when you’re getting
784	started on a problem no one has solved before. If you can’t beat a trivial solution, your
785	model is worthless—perhaps you’re using the wrong model or perhaps the problem
786	you’re tackling can’t even be approached with machine learning in the first place. Time
787	to go back to the drawing board.
788

790	
791	Things to keep in mind about model evaluation
792	Keep an eye out for the following when you’re choosing an evaluation protocol:
793	¡ Data representativeness—You want both your training set and test set to be rep-
794	
795	resentative of the data at hand. For instance, if you’re trying to classify images
796	of digits, and you’re starting from an array of samples where the samples are

802	
803	ordered by their class, taking the first 80% of the array as your training set and
804	the remaining 20% as your test set will result in your training set containing only
805	classes 0–7, whereas your test set contains only classes 8–9. This seems like a ridiculous mistake, but it’s surprisingly common. For this reason, you usually should
806	randomly shuffle your data before splitting it into training and test sets.
807	¡ The arrow of time—If you’re trying to predict the future given the past (for example, tomorrow’s weather, stock movements, and so on), you should not randomly
808	shuffle your data before splitting it because doing so will create a temporal leak:
809	your model will effectively be trained on data from the future. In such situations,
810	you should always make sure all data in your test set is posterior to the data in the
811	training set.
812	¡ Redundancy in your data—If some data points in your data appear twice (fairly
813	common with real-world data), then shuffling the data and splitting it into a
814	training set and a validation set will result in redundancy between the training
815	and validation sets. In effect, you’ll be testing on part of your training data, which
816	is the worst thing you can do! Make sure your training set and validation set are
817	disjoint.
818	Having a reliable way to evaluate the performance of your model is how you’ll be able
819	to monitor the tension at the heart of machine learning—between optimization and
820	generalization, underfitting and overfitting.

824	Improving model fit
825	To achieve the perfect fit, you must first overfit. Since you don’t know in advance where
826	the boundary lies, you must cross it to find it. Thus, your initial goal as you start working on a problem is to achieve a model that shows some generalization power, and that
827	is able to overfit. Once you have such a model, you’ll focus on refining generalization
828	by fighting overfitting.
829	There are three common problems you’ll encounter at this stage:
830	¡ Training doesn’t get started: your training loss doesn’t go down over time.
831	¡ Training gets started just fine, but your model doesn’t meaningfully generalize:
832	
833	you can’t beat the common-sense baseline you set.
834	¡ Training and validation loss both go down over time, and you can beat your
835	baseline, but you don’t seem to be able to overfit, which indicates you’re still
836	underfitting.

918	You have a model that fits, but for some reason your validation metrics aren’t improving at all. They remain no better than what a random classifier would achieve: your
919	model trains, but doesn’t generalize. What’s going on?
920	This is perhaps the worst machine learning situation you can find yourself in. It indicates that something is fundamentally wrong with your approach, and it may not be easy to tell

922	First, it may be that the input data you’re using simply doesn’t contain sufficient
923	information to predict your targets: the problem as formulated is not solvable. This is

929	model that makes the right assumptions about the problem is essential to achieve generalization: you should use the right architecture priors.
930	In the following chapters, you’ll learn about the best architectures to use for a
931	variety of data modalities—images, text, timeseries, and so on. In general, you should
932	always make sure to read up on architecture best practices for the kind of task you’re

1069	Dataset curation
1070	You’ve already learned that generalization in deep learning originates from the latent
1071	structure of your data. If your data makes it possible to smoothly interpolate between
1072	samples, then you will be able to train a deep learning model that generalizes. If your
1073	problem is overly noisy or fundamentally discrete, like, say, list sorting, deep learning
1074	will not help you. Deep learning is curve fitting, not magic.
1075	As such, it is essential that you make sure that you’re working with an appropriate
1076	dataset. Spending more effort and money on data collection almost always yields a much
1077	greater return on investment than spending the same on developing a better model:
1078	¡ Make sure you have enough data. Remember that you need a dense sampling of
1079	
1080	the input-cross-output space. More data will yield a better model. Sometimes,
1081	problems that seem impossible at first become solvable with a larger dataset.
1082	¡ Minimize labeling errors—visualize your inputs to check for anomalies, and
1083	
1084	proofread your labels.
1085	¡ Clean your data and deal with missing values (we cover this in the next chapter).
1086	¡ If you have many features and you aren’t sure which ones are actually useful, do
1087	
1088	feature selection.
1089	A particularly important way you can improve the generalization potential of your data
1090	is feature engineering. For most machine learning problems, feature engineering is a key
1091	ingredient for success. Let’s take a look.
1092	
1093	5.4.2
1094	
1095	Feature engineering
1096	Feature engineering is the process of using your own knowledge about the data and
1097	about the machine learning algorithm at hand (in this case, a neural network) to make
1098	the algorithm work better by applying hardcoded (non-learned) transformations to
1099	the data before it goes into the model. In many cases, it isn’t reasonable to expect a
1100	machine learning model to be able to learn from completely arbitrary data. The data
1101	needs to be presented to the model in a way that will make the model’s job easier.
1102	Let’s look at an intuitive example. Suppose you’re trying to develop a model that
1103	can take as input an image of a clock and can output the time of day (see figure 5.17).
1104	If you choose to use the raw pixels of the image as input data, then you have a difficult
1105	machine learning problem on your hands. You’ll need a convolutional neural network
1106	to solve it, and you’ll have to expend quite a bit of computational resources to train the
1107	network.
1108	But if you already understand the problem at a high level (you understand how
1109	humans read time on a clock face), then you can come up with much better input features for a machine learning algorithm: for instance, it’s easy to write a five-line Python
1110	script to follow the black pixels of the clock hands and output the (x, y) coordinates of
1111	the tip of each hand. Then a simple machine learning algorithm can learn to associate
1112	these coordinates with the appropriate time of day.

1151	You can go even further: do a coordinate change and express the (x, y) coordinates
1152	as polar coordinates with regard to the center of the image. Your input will become the

1156	That’s the essence of feature engineering: making a problem easier by expressing it
1157	in a simpler way. Make the latent manifold smoother, simpler, and better organized. It
1158	usually requires understanding the problem in depth.
1159	Before deep learning, feature engineering used to be the most important part of the
1160	machine learning workflow because classical shallow algorithms didn’t have hypothesis spaces rich enough to learn useful features by themselves. The way you presented
1161	the data to the algorithm was absolutely critical to its success. For instance, before
1162	convolutional neural networks became successful on the MNIST digit-classification
1163	problem, solutions were typically based on hardcoded features such as the number of
1164	loops in a digit image, the height of each digit in an image, a histogram of pixel values,
1165	and so on.
1166	Fortunately, modern deep learning removes the need for most feature engineering
1167	because neural networks are capable of automatically extracting useful features from
1168	raw data. Does this mean you don’t have to worry about feature engineering as long as
1169	you’re using deep neural networks? No, for two reasons:
1170	¡ Good features still allow you to solve problems more elegantly while using fewer
1171	
1172	resources. For instance, it would be ridiculous to solve the problem of reading a
1173	clock face using a convolutional neural network.
1174	¡ Good features let you solve a problem with far less data. The ability of deep-­
1175	
1176	learning models to learn features on their own relies on having lots of training
1177	data available; if you have only a few samples, then the information value in their
1178	features becomes critical.

1187	Using early stopping
1188	In deep learning, we always use models that are vastly overparameterized: they have
1189	way more degrees of freedom than the minimum necessary to fit to the latent manifold
1190	of the data. This overparameterization is not an issue because you never fully fit a deep
1191	learning model. Such a fit wouldn’t generalize at all. You will always interrupt training
1192	long before you’ve reached the minimum possible training loss.
1193	Finding the exact point during training where you’ve reached the most generalizable fit—the exact boundary between an underfit curve and an overfit curve—is one of
1194	the most effective things you can do to improve generalization.
1195	In the examples from the previous chapter, we would start by training our models for
1196	longer than needed to figure out the number of epochs that yielded the best validation
1197	metrics, then we would retrain a new model for exactly that number of epochs. This is
1198	pretty standard. However, it requires you to do redundant work, which can sometimes
1199	be expensive. Naturally, you could just save your model at the end of each epoch, then
1200	once you’ve found the best epoch, reuse the closest saved model you have. In Keras, it’s
1201	typical to do this with an EarlyStopping callback, which will interrupt training as soon as
1202	validation metrics have stopped improving, while remembering the best known model
1203	state. You’ll learn to use callbacks in chapter 7.

1207	Regularizing your model
1208	Regularization techniques are a set of best practices that actively impede the model’s ability to fit perfectly to the training data, with the goal of making the model perform better during validation. This is called “regularizing” the model because it tends to make
1209	the model simpler, more “regular,” its curve smoother, and more “generic”—thus less
1210	specific to the training set and better able to generalize by more closely approximating
1211	the latent manifold of the data. Keep in mind that “regularizing” a model is a process that should always be guided by an accurate evaluation procedure. You will only
1212	achieve generalization if you can measure it.
1213	Let’s review some of the most common regularization techniques and apply them in
1214	practice to improve the movie classification model from chapter 4.
1215	Reducing the network’s size
1216	
1217	You’ve already learned that a model that is too small will not overfit. The simplest way
1218	to mitigate overfitting is to reduce the size of the model (the number of learnable
1219	parameters in the model, determined by the number of layers and the number of
1220	units per layer). If the model has limited memorization resources, it won’t be able
1221	to simply memorize its training data. To minimize its loss, it will have to resort to
1222	learning compressed representations that have predictive power regarding the
1223	targets—precisely the type of representations we’re interested in. At the same time,
1224	keep in mind that you should use models that have enough parameters that they don’t
1225	underfit: your model shouldn’t be starved for memorization resources. There is a
1226	compromise to be found between too much capacity and not enough capacity.

1236	for your data. The general workflow to find an appropriate model size is to start with

1351	Adding weight regularization
1352	
1353	You may be familiar with the principle of Occam’s razor: given two explanations for
1354	something, the explanation most likely to be correct is the simplest one—the one
1355	that makes fewer assumptions. This idea also applies to the models learned by neural
1356	
1357	
1358	Improving generalization
1359	
1360	165
1361	
1362	networks: given some training data and a network architecture, multiple sets of weight
1363	values (multiple models) could explain the data. Simpler models are less likely to overfit
1364	than complex ones.
1365	A simple model in this context is a model where the distribution of parameter values
1366	has less entropy (or a model with fewer parameters, as you saw in the previous section).
1367	Thus a common way to mitigate overfitting is to put constraints on the complexity of a
1368	model by forcing its weights to take only small values, which makes the distribution of
1369	weight values more regular. This is called weight regularization, and it’s done by adding
1370	to the loss function of the model a cost associated with having large weights. This cost
1371	comes in two flavors:
1372	¡ L1 regularization—The cost added is proportional to the absolute value of the weight
1373	
1374	coefficients (the L1 norm of the weights).
1375	¡ L2 regularization—The cost added is proportional to the square of the value of the
1376	
1377	weight coefficients (the L2 norm of the weights). L2 regularization is also called
1378	weight decay in the context of neural networks. Don’t let the different name confuse you: weight decay is mathematically the same as L2 regularization.
1379	In Keras, weight regularization is added by passing weight regularizer instances to layers
1380	as keyword arguments. Let’s add L2 weight regularization to the movie review classification model.

1445	neural networks. Dropout, applied to a layer, consists of randomly dropping out (setting to zero) a number of output features of the layer during training. Let’s say a given
1446	layer would normally return a vector [0.2, 0.5, 1.3, 0.8, 1.1] for a given input

1555	This technique may seem strange and arbitrary. Why would this help reduce overfitting? Hinton says he was inspired by, among other things, a fraud-prevention mechanism used by banks:
1556	I went to my bank. The tellers kept changing and I asked one of them why. He said
1557	he didn’t know but they got moved around a lot. I figured it must be because it would
1558	require cooperation between employees to successfully defraud the bank. This made me
1559	realize that randomly removing a different subset of neurons on each example would
1560	prevent conspiracies and thus reduce overfitting.
1561	The core idea is that introducing noise in the output values of a layer can break up
1562	happenstance patterns that aren’t significant (what Hinton refers to as conspiracies),
1563	which the model will start memorizing if no noise is present.
1564	In Keras, you can introduce dropout in a model via the Dropout layer, which is
1565	applied to the output of the layer right before it. Let’s add two Dropout layers in the
1566	IMDB model to see how well they do at reducing overfitting.

1621	A deep neural network achieves generalization by learning a parametric model
1622	that can successfully interpolate between training samples. Such a model can be
1623	said to have learned the latent manifold of the training data. This is why deep
1624	learning models can only make sense of inputs that are very close to what they’ve
1625	seen during training.
1626	The fundamental problem in machine learning is the tension between optimization
1627	and generalization: to attain generalization, you must first achieve a good fit to the
1628	training data, but improving your model’s fit to the training data will inevitably
1629	start hurting generalization after a while. Every single deep learning best practice
1630	deals with managing this tension.
1631	The ability of deep learning models to generalize comes from the fact that they
1632	manage to learn to approximate the latent manifold of their data and can thus
1633	make sense of new inputs via interpolation.
1634	It’s essential to be able to accurately evaluate the generalization power of your
1635	model while you’re developing it. You have at your disposal an array of evaluation
1636	methods, from simple hold-out validation to K-fold cross-validation and iterated
1637	K-fold cross-validation with shuffling. Remember to always keep a completely

1646	¡ When you start working on a model, your goal is first to achieve a model that has
1647	some generalization power and that can overfit. Best practices to do this include
1648	tuning your learning rate and batch size, using better architecture priors, increasing model capacity, or simply training longer.
1649	¡ As your model starts overfitting, your goal switches to improving generalization
1650	through model regularization. You can reduce your model’s capacity, add dropout

154	Note on ethics
155	You may sometimes be offered ethically dubious projects, such as “building an AI that
156	rates the trustworthiness of someone from a picture of their face.” First of all, the
157	validity of the project is in doubt: it isn’t clear why trustworthiness would be reflected
158	on someone’s face. Second, such a task opens the door to all kinds of ethical problems. Collecting a dataset for this task would amount to recording the biases and
159	prejudices of the people who label the pictures. The models you would train on such
160	data would be merely encoding these same biases—into a black box algorithm, which
161	would give them a thin veneer of legitimacy. In a largely tech-illiterate society like
162	ours, “The AI algorithm said this person cannot be trusted” strangely appears to carry
163	more weight and objectivity than “John Smith said this person cannot be trusted”—
164	despite the former being a learned approximation of the latter. Your model would be
165	laundering and operationalizing at scale the worst aspects of human judgement, with
166	negative effects on the lives of real people.
167	Technology is never neutral. If your work has any impact on the world, then this impact
168	has a moral direction: technical choices are also ethical choices. Always be deliberate about the values you want your work to support.
